record.text: Agreed, and the block recursion also works, and they agree. It is still recurrent, also cube-free, no overlapping squares. But the blocks are no longer palindromes, and the string-rewriting account runs out of steam at omega.
Thinking about: the transfinite analogue of the Thue-Morse sequence.

I think this works without any difficulties: there's a base-2 Cantor normal form for ordinals, where every ordinal is uniquely represented as a finite sum of decreasing distinct powers of 2; thus for an ordinal alpha, t_alpha is the parity of the number of summands in this representation.

But to give a few hints: the block recursion works perfectly well. You start with w_0 = a, and then w_alpha+1 = (w_alpha)(\bar w_alpha), where we take the dual in the second half. Limits at limits. This agrees with binary-bit-count in binary ordinal arithmetic. Still recurrent, still cube-free.

record.text: This is a good list. In natural usage, I think we use the term to mean 1, since if you say you have a strategy, then I might say it is a losing strategy, because the opponent could xyz and win. So a losing strategy is one that might lose, and therefore will lose against optimal play.

An interesting question arose in my games class today. We discussed the concept of strategy, a complete set of instructions telling you how to move in any circumstance; a winning strategy is one for which you will invariably win by following those instructions, regardless of how the opponent plays.

1: A strategy that might lose.
2: A strategy that couldn't win. 
3: A strategy that must lose. 

I like 3 in part because it allows a losing strategy to become a winning strategy in the misère version of the game.

A drawing strategy is one ensuring a draw or better. (It might not ensure a draw if the opponent plays badly.) But what exactly does it mean to have a losing strategy? There are several alternatives, and I had disagreed with my students. What is your view?
